query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The wear resistance of HEA protective coatings is predominantly governed by the in-situ formation of a nano-structured, self-healing oxide layer during sliding. This oxide layer shields the underlying alloy from direct abrasive and adhesive damage.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited equiatomic or near-equiatomic HEA coating (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi) that contains high oxygen‐affinity elements (such as Cr or Al) and therefore is predisposed to form protective oxides under frictional heating.
generation.intervention: Perform sliding wear tests comparing two conditions: (1) an oxidizing environment (ambient air) where the oxide layer can form and (2) an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon) that minimizes oxidation. Alternatively, modify the alloy composition by adding (or omitting) a minor dopant such as Y or Hf known to stabilize the oxide layer.
generation.conditions: Wear tests conducted over a moderate temperature range (from room temperature up to around 800 °C) under controlled load and sliding speed, with careful control of ambient oxygen levels. This reflects typical operational conditions for wear-resistant applications in high-temperature components.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultra-thin, nanocrystalline oxide film (or glaze layer) that forms dynamically at the sliding interface.
generation.mechanism: Frictional contact and the consequent local heating trigger oxidation at the surface. A continuous oxide film forms and, by accommodating plastic deformation and reducing direct metal-to-metal contact, it lowers friction and mitigates wear from both abrasive and adhesive mechanisms.
generation.predicted_outcome: In the oxidizing environment (or for the composition promoting oxide stability), the coating will display lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates due to the protective, self-healing oxide layer. Conversely, in an inert atmosphere (or in alloys lacking oxidation‐promoting elements), the absence or degradation of the oxide layer will lead to higher friction and more rapid wear.
generation.baseline: HEA coatings tested under ambient conditions where a modest or naturally occurring oxide layer forms without any specific intervention to enhance its stability.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate for HEA coatings containing sufficient levels (typically >5 at.%) of oxide‐forming elements under wear and temperature conditions that promote moderate oxidation (up to around 800 °C). Beyond this range, either excessive oxidation or other high-temperature degradation mechanisms might prevail.
generation.uncertainty: The precise thickness, continuity, and mechanical properties of the in-situ oxide may vary with sliding speed, substrate temperature, and minor compositional differences, making quantitative prediction of wear rates challenging until detailed experimental characterization is performed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings with identical microstructures: one set is tested under ambient (oxidizing) conditions and the other under an inert atmosphere (argon) to suppress oxidation. Additionally, prepare a variant coating that has reduced content of high oxygen‐affinity elements. For each test, measure friction coefficients and wear rates, and analyze the worn surface for the presence and characteristics of the oxide layer (using SEM, EDS, and XPS).
measurements: Surface oxide layer thickness and composition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings tested in an oxidizing environment do not show statistically lower wear rates or friction coefficients compared to those tested in an inert atmosphere – or if reducing the oxide‐forming element content does not degrade wear performance – the hypothesis that the in-situ oxide layer governs wear resistance would be falsified.

Wear-related energy and material loss cost over 2500 Billion Euro per year. Traditional wisdom suggests that high-strength materials reveal low wear rates, yet, their plastic deformation mechanisms also influence their wear performance. High strength and homogeneous deformation behavior, which allow accommodating plastic strain without cracking or localized brittle fracture, are crucial for developing wear-resistant metals. Here, we present an approach to achieve superior wear resistance via in-situ formation of a strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surface during wear, by reaction of the metal surface with its oxidative environment, a principle that we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. We design a TiNbZr-Ag alloy that forms an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface layer upon dry sliding. The strong (2.4 GPa yield strength) and deformable (homogeneous deformation to 20% strain) nanocomposite surface reduces the wear rate of the TiNbZr-Ag alloy by an order of magnitude.
